x.ASV: Maschil of Asaph. Give ear, O my people, to my law: Incline your ears to the words of my mouth.
x.Darby: An instruction. Of Asaph. Give ear, O my people, to my law; incline your ears to the words of my mouth.
x.KJV: Maschil of Asaph. Give ear, O my people, to my law: incline your ears to the words of my mouth.
x.YLT: An Instruction of Asaph. Give ear, O my people, to my law, Incline your ear to sayings of my mouth.

nt: The superscription to this psalm identifies it as a **maskil**. Since the meaning of this word is not certain, you may wish to represent it in its Hebrew form and spell it the way it sounds in your language. See the discussion of that term in the Introduction to Psalms.
הַאֲזִ֣ינָ⁠ה עַ֭מִּ⁠י תּוֹרָתִ֑⁠י הַטּ֥וּ אָ֝זְנְ⁠כֶ֗ם לְ⁠אִמְרֵי־פִֽ⁠י

These two phrases mean basically the same thing. The second emphasizes the meaning of the first by repeating the same idea with different words. Hebrew poetry was based on this kind of repetition. If it would be helpful to your readers, you could combine the phrases and express the emphasis in another way. Another approach would be to connect the phrases with a word that shows that the second phrase is repeating the first one, not saying something additional. See how your team has decided to translate parallel phrases in the Psalms and follow that approach here and throughout this psalm. Alternate translation: [Hear my teaching, my people; yes, listen to the words of my mouth]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **teaching**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [Listen to what I teach you]

Asaph is using this possessive form **my people** to indicate that he is addressing the Israelites as a leader or teacher among them, not to indicate that they belong to him personally. If it would be helpful in your language, you could express this idea in another way. Alternate translation: [fellow Israelites] or [people of Israel]

Asaph is speaking of paying careful attention to his teaching as if his audience could physically **incline** their **ears** toward him in order to listen better. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [pay close attention] or [listen carefully]

Here, **the words of my mouth** represents what a person says. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [to what I say]

x.ASV: I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter dark sayings of old,
x.Darby: I will open my mouth in a parable; I will utter riddles from of old,
x.KJV: I will open my mouth in a parable: I will utter dark sayings of old:
x.YLT: I open with a simile my mouth, I bring forth hidden things of old,

nt: אֶפְתְּחָ֣ה בְ⁠מָשָׁ֣ל פִּ֑⁠י אַבִּ֥יעָה חִ֝יד֗וֹת מִנִּי־קֶֽדֶם

See the note on [78:1](../078/001.md) or in the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on translating parallelisms. Alternate translation: [I will open my mouth in parables, yes, I will sing about hidden things from the past]

Asaph is using **I will open my mouth** as a common expression of the culture to mean “I will speak” or “I will begin to teach.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will speak] or [I will begin to teach]

A **parable** is a type of teaching that uses comparisons, stories, or wise sayings to communicate deeper truths. If your readers would not be familiar with this concept, you could use a more general term. Alternate translation: [in wise sayings] or [in instructive stories]

If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **parables** and **riddles**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [my mouth in symbolic sayings; I will pour out what is difficult to understand from antiquity] or [my mouth by speaking metaphorically; I will pour out enigmatic sayings from antiquity]

Asaph is speaking of sharing wisdom as if he were **pouring out riddles** like liquid from a container. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression from your culture or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [I will utter riddles] or [I will proclaim mysteries]

x.ASV: Which we have heard and known, And our fathers have told us.
x.Darby: Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us:
x.KJV: Which we have heard and known, and our fathers have told us.
x.YLT: That we have heard and do know, And our fathers have recounted to us.

nt: The terms **heard** and **learned** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [These are things that we know well, things]

Asaph is speaking of earlier generations of Israelites as if they were **fathers**. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [that our forefathers] or [that those who came before us]

x.ASV: We will not hide them from their children, Telling to the generation to come the praises of Jehovah, And his strength, and his wondrous works that he hath done.
x.Darby: We will not hide [them] from their sons, shewing forth to the generation to come the praises of Jehovah, and his strength, and his marvellous works which he hath done.
x.KJV: We will not hide them from their children, shewing to the generation to come the praises of the Lord, and his strength, and his wonderful works that he hath done.
x.YLT: We do not hide from their sons, To a later generation recounting praises of Jehovah, And His strength, and His wonders that He hath done.

nt: Asaph is emphasizing a positive meaning by using a negative word, **not**, together with a mild expression that is the opposite of the intended meaning. If it would be helpful in your language, you could emphasize the positive meaning in a strong way. Alternate translation: [We will certainly tell these things to their descendants]
If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **praises**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [about the praiseworthy deeds of Yahweh]

The phrase **his strength, and his wonders** expresses a single idea. The word **strength** tells more about **wonders**. If it would be more natural in your language, you could express this meaning in a different way. Alternate translation: [his powerful wonders] or [the mighty miracles]

x.ASV: For he established a testimony in Jacob, And appointed a law in Israel, Which he commanded our fathers, That they should make them known to their children;
x.Darby: For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children;
x.KJV: For he established a testimony in Jacob, and appointed a law in Israel, which he commanded our fathers, that they should make them known to their children:
x.YLT: And He raiseth up a testimony in Jacob, And a law hath placed in Israel, That He commanded our fathers, To make them known to their sons.

nt: If your language does not use abstract nouns for the ideas of **testimony** and **law**, you could express the same ideas in other ways. Alternate translation: [what he decreed and commanded] or [his requirements and commands]

Here, **Jacob** and **Israel** represent all the descendants of the patriarch Jacob, the Israelite nation. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [among the people of Jacob and … a law among the people of Israel] or [among the descendants of Jacob and … a law among the descendants of Israel]

x.Darby: That the generation to come might know [them], the children that should be born; that they might rise up and tell [them] to their children,

x.YLT: So that a later generation doth know, Sons who are born, do rise and recount to their sons,

nt: **So that** marks the rest of verses 6–8 as the goal or purpose of verse five. Use a connector in your language that makes it clear that this is the purpose. Alternate translation: [He commanded this in order that the generation to come]
לְמַ֤עַן יֵדְע֨וּ ׀ דּ֣וֹר אַ֭חֲרוֹן בָּנִ֣ים יִוָּלֵ֑דוּ

The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [so that the generation to come might know his decrees, and so that the children not yet born might also know them]

The psalmist is using **rise up** as a common expression of the culture to mean “take action” or “come along.” He does not mean that the children will literally stand up. If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they in their turn will tell] or [and they will then tell]

x.ASV: That they might set their hope in God, And not forget the works of God, But keep his commandments,
x.Darby: And that they might set their hope inGod, and not forget the works ofGod, but observe his commandments;
x.KJV: That they might set their hope in God, and not forget the works of God, but keep his commandments:
x.YLT: And place in God their confidence, And forget not the doings of God, But keep His commands.

nt: The psalmist is speaking of **confidence** as if it were something that could be physically **placed** in a secure location. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [And they would trust in God] or [And they would rely on God]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **confidence**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [And they would hope in God] or [And they would confidently trust in God]

x.ASV: And might not be as their fathers, A stubborn and rebellious generation, A generation that set not their heart aright, And whose spirit was not stedfast with God.
x.Darby: And might not be as their fathers, a stubborn and rebellious generation, a generation that prepared not their heart, and whose spirit was not stedfast withGod.

x.YLT: And they are not like their fathers, A generation apostate and rebellious, A generation! it hath not prepared its heart, Nor stedfast with God is its spirit.

nt: The terms **stubborn** and **rebellious** mean similar things. The psalmist is using the two terms together for emphasis. If it would be clearer for your readers, you could express the emphasis with a single phrase. Alternate translation: [a very obstinate generation] or [an extremely defiant generation]

Here, **heart** represents the inner disposition and loyalty of a person. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [who were not inwardly loyal] or [whose inner disposition was not right]

Here, **spirit** represents the inner person or will. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they were not committed and faithful to God]

x.ASV: The children of Ephraim, being armed and carrying bows, Turned back in the day of battle.
x.Darby: The sons of Ephraim, armed bowmen, turned back in the day of battle.
x.KJV: The children of Ephraim, being armed, and carrying bows, turned back in the day of battle.
x.YLT: Sons of Ephraim--armed bearers of bow, Have turned in a day of conflict.

nt: The psalmist is using **turned back on the day of battle** as a common expression of the culture to mean “retreated in battle” or “fled when they should have fought.” If this phrase does not have that meaning for your readers, you could use a comparable expression from your language that does have that meaning, or you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [fled when they should have fought] or [retreated instead of fighting]

The psalmist is using the term **day** to refer to a specific time. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when it was time to fight] or [at the time of battle]

x.Darby: They kept not the covenant ofGod, and refused to walk in his law;

See the note on [78:1](../078/001.md) or the Introduction to the Psalms for more information on how to translate parallelisms. Alternate translation: [They did not keep the covenant with God; indeed, they refused to obey his law]

The psalmist is using this possessive form, **the covenant of God**, to mean the covenant that God had made with the Israelites. It may be helpful to clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [the covenant that God had made with them] or [God’s covenant]

The psalmist is speaking of obeying God’s law as if it were a path one could **walk** on. If it would be helpful in your language, you could state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [and they refused to obey his law]

x.ASV: And they forgat his doings, And his wondrous works that he had showed them.
x.Darby: And forgot his doings, and his marvellous works which he had shewn them.
x.KJV: And forgat his works, and his wonders that he had shewed them.
x.YLT: And they forget His doings, And His wonders that He shewed them.

nt: The psalmist is not distinguishing the **wonders that he had shown them** from other wonderful things that God had not shown them. The psalmist is reminding the people about the character of God’s deeds that they forgot. Be sure that this is clear in your translation. Alternate translation: [which were wonderful things that he had shown them]

x.ASV: Marvellous things did he in the sight of their fathers, In the land of Egypt, in the field of Zoan.

nt: The word **Zoan** is the name of a city.

Here, **their fathers** represents their ancestors who were present to see the marvelous things. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [when their ancestors were present] or [while their ancestors were watching]

nt: The point of this comparison is that just as **a heap** is a vertical structure, so **the waters** stood upright. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he made the waters stand upright like a solid wall]

x.ASV: In the day-time also he led them with a cloud, And all the night with a light of fire.
x.Darby: And he led them with a cloud in the daytime, and all the night with the light of fire.

nt: The psalmist is leaving out some of the words that in many languages a sentence would need in order to be complete. You can supply these words from the context if that would be clearer in your language. Alternate translation: [and all the night he led them with the light of fire]

By **the cloud** and **the light of fire**, the psalmist means the pillar of cloud and the pillar of fire that guided Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 13:21–22). You could indicate this explicitly in your translation if that would be helpful to your readers. Alternate translation: [with the pillar of cloud … with the pillar of fire]

x.ASV: He clave rocks in the wilderness, And gave them drink abundantly as out of the depths.
x.Darby: He clave rocks in the wilderness, and gave [them] drink as out of the depths, abundantly;
x.KJV: He clave the rocks in the wilderness, and gave them drink as out of the great depths.
x.YLT: He cleaveth rocks in a wilderness, And giveth drink--as the great deep.

nt: The pronoun **He** refers to God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [God split open]

The point of this comparison is that just as **the deep** has limitless water, so God provided limitless water for his people. If it would be helpful in your language, you could make this point explicitly. Alternate translation: [and he gave them water as limitless as the deep]

The psalmist says **and he gave drink abundantly as the deep** as an overstatement for emphasis. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a different way to express the emphasis. Alternate translation: [and he gave them an enormous amount of water to drink]

x.ASV: Yet went they on still to sin against him, To rebel against the Most High in the desert.

nt: The pronoun **they** refers to the Israelites, the ancestors of those whom the psalmist is addressing. If it would be helpful in your language, you could clarify this for your readers. Alternate translation: [And the Israelite people added] or [And those ancestors added]

The psalmist uses the word **And** here to indicate a contrast between God’s gracious provision and the people’s sinful response. In your translation, indicate this contrast in a way that is natural in your language. Alternate translation: [But they added still to sin against him] or [Yet they added still to sin against him]

x.KJV: And they tempted God in their heart by asking meat for their lust.

Alternate translation: [And they tested God in their hearts when they asked for food for their appetite]

Here, **hearts** represents the inner thoughts and attitudes. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use an equivalent expression or plain language. Alternate translation: [in their minds] or [inwardly]

If your language does not use an abstract noun for the idea of **appetite**, you could express the same idea in another way. Alternate translation: [for what they craved] or [for what they desired to eat]

The Israelites are speaking of God providing food as if he were **arranging a table** for a meal. If it would be helpful in your language, you could use a comparable expression or state the meaning plainly. Alternate translation: [provide food for us]

The people are speaking of themselves in the third person as **his people** to acknowledge their relationship with God. If it would be helpful in your language, you could translate this in the first person. Alternate translation: [for us, his people]
